utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, we had reached the events in Donje Obrinje that you had described. In Gornje Obrinje -- in Gornje Obrinje, you were in contact with KDOM; right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contact with KDOM you're referring to was on that morning, the 29th of September. Before we arrived in Gornje Obrinje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says on page 7, paragraph 3 of your first statement, that you were informed about this by KDOM, American KDOM, that you got this information from them. And when you came to Gornje Obrinje, did you talk to any of the eyewitnesses?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it's not correct that we were informed by KDOM. We confirmed the incident with KDOM. More specifically, I was informed of an unconfirmed report on the 28th of September that killings might have taken place in Gornje Obrinje village. And on the 29th, before travelling into Drenica where an offensive was still taking place, myself and my colleagues -- my colleague, together with a journalist from The New York Times, went to the KDOM office to ask two questions. One, whether something had happened in Gornje Obrinje, and they said yes without providing details; and secondly, which road we might take to best avoid land-mines, because in the last day or two, I believe the 26th, a Canadian KDOM vehicle had struck a land-mine. And indeed on -- I believe the 29th or the 30th, an ICRC vehicle also hit a land-mine, and we wanted to be sure that this didn't happen to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But my question was whether you then talked to some of the eyewitnesses in Gornje Obrinje.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We spoke with every possible person that was in some way helpful to understanding the case. I'm sorry, are you referring to KDOM specifically?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I had asked you previously about KDOM, and I quoted your statement of the 28th of September. The second question I put to you now was whether you had talked to any of the eyewitnesses. My understanding is that you had talked to eyewitnesses; right? So -- see, in your statement on page 7, that is the first statement you gave, it says: "Some of the people who told us what had happened in their view escaped when the police came. They had not been eyewitnesses of the event." That is to say that, over here, you state that you had talked to persons who had not been eyewitnesses of the event. So it's not that you saw the event take place or the people you talked to. So you did not talk to any of the eyewitnesses who had actually seen the event take place. Let me remind you. It is the penultimate paragraph on page 7. "They were not eyewitnesses of this event." That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. There were no -- nobody saw the killings directly, but we spoke with the individuals who experienced and witnessed the circumstances around the killings, who could explain for us what happened prior to that moment and after that moment. So we were able to reconstruct the incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but on the basis of what you said you could reconstruct, you mentioned yesterday that in that fighting around Gornje Obrinje, 14 policemen had died. Doesn't that show, beyond any doubt, that this was serious, heavy fighting?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without any doubt, there was fighting in and around Gornje Obrinje. As I mentioned yesterday, the KLA had a base in the nearby village of Likovac. However, none of that, in our opinion and based on the facts, was relevant to the killings of the Delijaj family. There were 21 members of the family killed. Fourteen of them were in the forest. That I mentioned yesterday. And they were all women and children --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've explained that. Let's not waste time with this. Let's not waste time with this. You've explained that. I'm trying to clarify one particular point with you, and that is that, quite simply, without any proof, without any conversations with the direct eyewitnesses of this event - and this event involved the killing of 14 policemen - you explained this event as a crime committed by the Serb police; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the facts have led us to that conclusion, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I could not establish what kind of facts you had, because you were talking to people who were not eyewitnesses, as you can see, and you are drawing conclusions nevertheless. Can you make any comment with regard to this: My associates got by e-mail a letter from George Tintor from New York, a compatriot of yours. Can you make a comment with regard to what he says here: [In English] "[Previous translation continues] ... that Abrahams was working hand in glove with NATO propagandists to smear the Serbs. Abrahams made his statement to CNN just four days after the bombing began and only a day after the US government began its atrocity/genocide propaganda blitz on the Sunday morning news shows in America. Even if Abrahams' allegation were true, it would have been impossible for a person in his position, sitting in New York, to have gathered and verified sufficient evidence in such a short and chaotic period of time to make the claims he made." [Interpretation] He also refers to a letter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness deal with this. Mr. Milosevic, you are putting matters which the witness should deal with. Remember, you're asking questions. But before you do, tell us, if you would, who this Mr. George Tintor is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm not familiar with that name, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Milosevic, who is this George Tintor?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a compatriot of his, a New Yorker. I wanted to read a letter that he had sent to CNN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Let the witness deal with this, insofar as it's of any assistance to the Court: The view of some inhabitant of New York is apparently that you were hand in glove with NATO propagandists to smear the Serbs, and then there's some point here made that even if you were sitting in New York, it would have been impossible for you to have gathered and verified sufficient evidence. So there are two points made by this Mr. Tintor, whoever he may be. You must have the opportunity, since they've been read out, to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, regarding the allegation of sitting in New York, I can only stress again what I said yesterday, which is that we conducted our research in the field. This report on the Gornje Obrinje killings was based on more than three weeks of research, as were the other reports. So we were very cautious not to sit in New York and judge the situation from a distance. As for the hand-in-glove conspiracies, you know, again I think the best response is to point to our research, and our reports have been critical of NATO. Our report on NATO even had a different perspective than the ICTY's findings on NATO, the preliminary investigation that the Prosecutor's office conducted, and I believe that we've been balanced in this, in documenting this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you say to this, to what he wrote in his letter to CNN on that day: [In English] "Abrahams' comments on the situation in Kosovo were shameful. He accuses the Serbs of systematically committing atrocities against the ethnic Albanians, yet his charges are based on no hard evidence but on reports from human rights activists and journalists in Kosovo. Mr. Abrahams fails to mention that these activists and journalists are probably all ethnic Albanian. He uses terms like 'pattern,' 'history,' and 'consistent stories' to support his allegation. In general, Mr. Abrahams' presentation seemed too sleek and too well orchestrated to be plausible. It seems that his main purpose was to help the US administration in its desperate attempt to justify the bombing of Serbia. President Clinton knows well that without testimonies like Mr. Abrahams', public support for the bombing would evaporate." [Interpretation] Do you believe that this is true, what George Tintor says, at the time when you were making statements in New York about what was going on in Kosovo? And I am talking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I respect my fellow New Yorkers, but I do not know who this person is. Still, I can respond to his allegations. First of all, I categorically reject the allegation that we accused Serbs of committing atrocities. That is a misrepresentation of our findings. We accused the Serbian and Yugoslav governments, or Serbian and Yugoslav forces, of committing violations, and that is a crucial, crucial distinction I want to make, not to attack the Serbian nation or the Serbian people. Secondly, this report, "Under Orders," has more than 60 pages of footnotes. All of the other reports have a similarly large number of footnotes. And if you look, a large percentage of these footnotes are our interviews in the field. We gave the date and the place of the interview. So it is simply not true that we sit in our offices and concoct or imagine atrocities or use the information from journalists or local human rights activists. Of course we would use their information as a lead or as a confirmation of something we have also documented but not as a primary source.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, when you cite quotations from persons that are critical of testimony from witnesses, that criticism, in my view, would be more credible and more believable if you knew something more about the person, if you could tell us something more. For example here, George Tintor. He is simply, as the Presiding Judge says, an inhabitant of New York. It would be much more credible, and I think the cross-examination would be much stronger if you had something more to say about the persons whose works you are citing. Here we have Mr. Abrahams. You have criticisms of his testimony. You're entitled to that. But we do know about Mr. Abrahams. What I am suggesting to you is that in future, when you have these quotations, let your researchers tell you a little more about the persons who are making these criticisms.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your suggestion. I think that the most important thing here is that the facts that he quotes, that is to say that Mr. George Tintor quotes, are undeniable. They are obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What facts? What facts, Mr. Milosevic? It was a series of allegations against the witness. No facts at all. Now, Mr. Abrahams, there's a second part of that quotation from Mr. Tintor -- just a moment -- from Mr. Tintor which is probably no longer on the transcript on the screen, but it was this -- and no doubt it's a suggestion which is being adopted by the accused, and you should have a chance to deal with it. The suggestion is that your purpose was to assist the United States administration in justifying their bombing. Now, that is a discussion which is made, and you should have the opportunity to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I reject that allegation. I think our reports have been critical of US foreign policy. We were shouting about human rights violations in Kosovo throughout the 1990s, shouts that were falling on deaf ears in Western capitals. And we then criticised the conduct of the NATO bombing without -- and Human Rights Watch never -- never explicitly -- or never called for the bombing. We called for economic and political action, resolute action, to halt the abuses in Kosovo, but I believe our criticisms of the Western governments and NATO are the best response that I can provide to the allegation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, when I refer to "facts," I mean the facts that information is second -- the information gathered is secondhand information from so-called activists and from journalists who were involved in the media campaign and the media war against Yugoslavia. So absolutely this kind of credibility cannot be considered seriously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take another example. Mr. Abrahams, would you like to comment on this? This is a comment from January 29th: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... categorically rejected Yugoslav government claims that the January 15th attack on Racak were either Kosovo Liberation Army soldiers killed in combat or civilians caught in crossfire." [Interpretation] You are talking about some kind of a detailed investigation of yours. How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are you quoting from? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am quoting a report of Human Rights Watch: "Investigation Finds Yugoslav Forces Guilty of War Crimes in Racak, Kosovo." I'm quoting their very own report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just indicate -- just indicate which report it is and we can find it. Mr. Abrahams, can you help us? A reference to the 29th of January.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's in this report, Your Honour, on page 76.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is this Exhibit 198, is that right, "A Week of Terror in Drenica"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 76.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know whether that's it. I quoted what it says here. So you and your activists and your journalists, you give yourselves the right to say that you have carried out a detailed investigation. And it says here: [In English] "The investigation, the organisation, accused organisation," it means Human Rights Watch, "accused Serbian Special Police forces and the Yugoslav army of indiscriminately attacking civilians, torturing detainees, and committing summary executions. The evidence suggests that government forces had direct order to kill village inhabitants over the age of 15." [Interpretation] Please, where did you get this kind of evidence from? Everything that came up afterwards in connection with Racak showed that this was a deception that was organised by William Walker. And this is not true, and that indeed it was members of the KLA who were killed.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report - and I believe you're quoting the press release to the report - was based on our field research. As I mentioned yesterday, a Human Rights Watch consultant named Gordana Igric spent one week researching in and around Racak and wrote this report based on her work in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question is the following: Do you think that Human Rights Watch, by using journalists and activists, could have obtained for itself the right to speak about assessments, to say whether it was a crime or not, whether there was guilt involved, guilt on whose part, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We would not base our findings on the work of journalists or activists. We base our findings on our research in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said, when I asked you about how Human Rights Watch was financed, you said that every donation over $5.000 is specially registered. And it contributes to a substantial budget, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And do you agree that a person has to be pretty rich, quite rich, in order to be able to give donations of over $5.000 to an organisation of this kind?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either quite rich or very concerned about the issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doesn't it seem to you that this organisation is actually an organisation that is financed by the rich and it helps the rich put the poor under their own control, that that is the core of this organisation that does this under the guise of human rights protection? That is to say that the rich finance this organisation in order to have the poor put under their control.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe that's the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that this is a new type of colonialism and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. This is taking this well beyond the bounds of possible cross-examination. Now, ask some other questions, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, linked to you yourself, Mr. Abrahams, how come that you as an American, as a New Yorker, as a man who deals in the field of human rights in the organisation called Human Rights Watch, that you take greater care of the human rights of Albanians in Yugoslavia than you do about human rights of Americans in America?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Irrelevant. Yes, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to how many homeless there are, how many hungry people there are in America, how many of the coloured population --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we said you had an hour. If you waste time with irrelevant questions like this, the cross-examination will be brought to an end now. Now, it's a matter for you whether you want to continue with proper questions or irrelevant questions. If you go on with irrelevant questions, the examination will be brought to a close.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, we are dealing here with credibility and the purpose of the organisation Human Rights Watch. It is not an irrelevant question, but a pertinent, relevant one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is quite irrelevant. Do you want to ask more questions or do you want to bring this to a close?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a great deal of other questions, Mr. May, to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, go on with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about Orahovac. Do you know that -- the KLA, you say, attempted to take control of Orahovac. How many Serbs, inhabitants of Orahovac, therefore civilians, disappeared in those two days while the KLA was in control of Orahovac? Page 12, paragraph 3, there you yourself say that 40 Serb civilians went missing during those two days.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The KLA did briefly take Orahovac, and 85 Serbs, civilians, were taken into detention. But after a few days, if my memory serves me correctly, I believe 45 of them were released, and 35 of them remained in custody. And these 35 people are still missing today, and my personal opinion is that they are probably no longer alive. And Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this is one of the most serious incidents from 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, there you have it. They didn't kill 40, but 35 Serb civilians in those two days. And you claim and say that in the fighting in Orahovac, 42 persons were killed of Albanian ethnicity. So in the fighting, 42 members of the KLA were killed and 40 Serb civilians disappeared, and you yourself say that they were probably killed because nothing is known of their fate until the present day. Why do you equate the victims that lost their lives in fighting with the civilians that were abducted and later killed without any chance of life? Why now, in that specific case, where we have an attack by the KLA on Orahovac and the killing of civilians on one side and members of the KLA on the other side, a terrorist organisation, you lay the blame at the door of the government forces, as you call them, that is to say, the army and the police of Yugoslavia? Who attacked whom on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I believe the KLA attempted to take control of Orahovac, starting from the town of Malisevo, which they controlled at that time. I do not believe that we are trying to equate these abuses, and we quite clearly condemn the abductions and what I would call the disappearances of the 35 Serbian civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree that you're not trying to equate this. On the contrary, you hold the blame with the Yugoslav authorities, the authorities of Serbia. So you're not equating this in any way. But let's go back to your own claims with respect to Gornje Obrinje, where you say that 14 policemen were killed and that there was heavy fighting, and your conclusion was that the Serb forces, as you refer to them, responded disproportionately. What, in your opinion, would be considered proportionate? How many policemen would have had to have been killed for you to have considered it to be proportional?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, the number of victims among armed forces, whether it's 14 or 1.400, does not justify the targeting or the killing of one civilian. And I am thoroughly and completely convinced that the members of the Delijaj family were not combatants. They were hiding in the woods, they appeared to have been shot in the head, and I found no evidence to suggest that they were involved in military activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't find any evidence either of who they were killed by, from whose fire power; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our conclusion was Serbian forces, which is admittedly somewhat vague because we were -- we did not find the evidence to point the finger directly at the special police forces or the anti-terrorist units. And again, we will not make an allegation, a strong allegation, without such evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you base your claims on the fact that they were Albanians who were killed, and when it was Albanians who were killed, they must have been killed by Serbs. That is your - how shall I put it? - method of reaching conclusions. Now, do you know how many Albanian terrorists of the KLA killed Albanians in 1998 and 1999? Do you know how many Albanians were killed?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I reject the assertion that we assume anything. On the contrary; we, if anything, we assume that a violation has not taken place. We try to find all the evidence to disprove our concern and conduct our investigations with this critical approach in mind. Regarding your question on Albanian victims, in other words, Albanian-on-Albanian violence, I do not have a precise figure, but it is certain that ethnic Albanians were killed, intimidated, physically abused. Mostly these are individuals who were considered to be collaborators with the Serbian state. I am not justifying; I'm explaining the logic. And so this was definitely a problem, and we have reported on that in our report after the NATO bombing in August 1999, the report called "Abuses Against Serbs and Roma in the New Kosovo." There's a section that documents Albanian-on-Albanian crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but as to the victims on the Serb side, you spoke about that after June 1999, that is to say, about these mass crimes. And when you say that they killed ethnic Albanians who were considered collaborators, in a state in which they lived, do you, with your criteria of human rights, accept -- can you accept, for example, that postmen or foresters or physicians working in state hospitals, only because they work for the state authorities in hospitals, forestry reserves, and so on, can be killed just like that, with justified political reasons, saying that they collaborated by carrying on with their profession and doing their job in the country and state they lived in? What kind of criteria are these? Can you accept those? Are they acceptable criteria?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it's not true that we only reported on Serbian abuses after the NATO bombing. Our report from 1998 includes an entire chapter on violations by the KLA. We issued other statements as well about the abduction of Serbian journalists and so on. Regarding your question, absolutely not. We don't accept this. Albanians who chose to work for the state, who even chose to work for the police, they have that right. They're citizens of Yugoslavia. And we condemn the violations against them, and we did so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right. You've just said this in rhetorical fashion. You have come here to testify for alleged war crimes. Did you give testimony about war crimes of the KLA and their leaders, committed by them, in view of the experience you've gained and in view of the fact that you yourself said yesterday that they did commit crimes? Did you make that kind of testimony, referring to their crimes?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the information that we published on that issue was given to the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means you treated both sides in completely the same way; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. In what respect?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in the sense of elementary morals and ethics, in the sense of accusing the legal forces fighting against terrorism and with respect to the crimes perpetrated by the terrorist groups in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we made honest efforts to be as objective as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the article that you were looking at yesterday, dated the 5th of August, 1998, you wrote the following, words to this effect, and I'm quoting you: "Washington is missing the point that there will be no stability in the Balkans for as long as Milosevic is in power." Now, this stability, does that mean that there will be no occupation? What I mean is that one of the previous witnesses, Paddy Ashdown, who is now an occupying chief in Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, first of all, you're supposed to be asking questions, let me remind you. Secondly, we don't want abuse of any sort of anybody here. Now, what's the question? Perhaps, Mr. Abrahams, we can allow you to deal with the quotation. I don't know if you remember it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you like to explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. Yes, I wrote this in Op. Ed. That was published in the International Herald Tribune, and I stand 100 per cent behind my words. It was my personal opinion and the opinion of the organisation that the Balkans would remain instable while Milosevic remained in power. And this was not a political view that we then sought to back up or to buttress by finding the facts. This was a conclusion that we reached based on our research in the field, that there was a cycle of violence, a cycle of abuse; there was a continued reluctance to resolve conflicts in a peaceful manner; there was a tendency to antagonise and provoke; there was even, if you indulge a political -- I mean, the opinion that conflict was used for political means. So based on that, we concluded -- or I concluded this line, that stability was impossible as long as that government remained in power.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you differentiate between cause and effect?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you -- can you clarify the question? In general or in this instance here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. First I mean in general terms. Do you make a difference between cause and effect?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How, then, was there nothing of what you have spoken about until the start of the violent criminal behaviour precisely at the beginning of 1998 and in 1999? How come up until then? The government was in power up until. Then, it had been in power for a full ten years up until that time. How, then, that there was nothing? It was testimony only when the terrorist attacks began and the killings of policemen, postmen, foresters, civilians and so on. Suddenly this government became a sort of criminal government which was committing crimes in protecting its citizens from crimes in terrorism.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kosovo was an extremely violent place for the past decade, and our reports throughout the 1990s document a series and a pattern of abuses and violations. So it's not true that criticisms only came in 1998. We were reporting on these violations prior to the armed conflict and intensified our reporting when the abuses themselves became more intense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right. You yourself, in your report, spoke about the exodus of Serbs in the 1970s and 1980s and so on. Now, how come this exodus took place, and what happened, in fact, with all that? Did you think about these things? Did you collect information, facts and figures about that? Who exerted violence against whom? Why this exodus of Serbs in those years? At least, what you referred to.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Human Rights Watch has addressed that issue, albeit in a historical way because we were not conducting research in the field at that time, but we did conclude that there was some discrimination against the Serbian population of Kosovo in the '80s, in the 1980s. However, we also concluded that this discrimination was nowhere near the extent or intensity of the claims made in Belgrade. I'm referring most specifically to the infamous memorandum of the Academy of Science, which said that genocide was being committed in Kosovo against Serbs. We always believed that this was a gross exaggeration. And while problems did exist, it did not reach that level by any means. And in fact, we also concluded that many Serbs left Kosovo for economic reasons. Kosovo was the poorest region, the poorest province of former Yugoslavia and that this poverty had a very negative effect on inter-ethnic relations and particularly that many Serbs left in order to seek a better life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you say in the memorandum put out by the Academy of Science, which is the highest scientific institution in Serbia, that they exaggerated, what about -- did your Human Rights Watch go to visit the Academy of Science and ask for an explanation, the arguments put forward, and therefore to publicize this and to test it according to your criteria, that perhaps it wasn't exaggeration? Perhaps they were observations based on facts. Did you do that or did you not?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our research in Kosovo began in 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say, on page 3 of your second statement, that is to say that you claim that most of the reports of the Human Rights Watch refer to the abuse of human rights or war crimes which were perpetrated, as you say, by the Serb or Yugoslav authorities because they express an intensity of violation in the field, on the ground. You wrote words to that effect. Do you not feel it to be too obvious and -- that there is too much compatibility between your statement and this false indictment that was raised here? Even when we come to the order in which all these things were set out. You analysed the indictment. You said this yourself. You wrote the statement yourself. So what I'm asking you now is: Do you not seem to feel that this coincidence between the indictment and your statement is very great?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it's not correct that I analysed the indictment. I conducted research --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's what you wrote.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the correct answer is that I conducted research for the Kosovo case. As for the similarities, as you stated, I can only say that the facts led us to our conclusions, the facts as we researched them in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, don't you feel that it is precisely these arguments presented by you, as indeed the argumentation of the indictment is, in essence, as is this trial; that is to say that the main goal is to justify the crimes perpetrated by NATO against a sovereign country? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have been over this. It is not for the witness to comment on the purpose of the trial. He is merely here to give evidence. You have made these allegations about justification of the NATO bombing as a reason for his evidence. He's given you his answer. He says it's completely untrue. Now, there's no point going over it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you claim that it is untrue that your statements were made-to-order, commissioned?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I claim that this is untrue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that you did research into the exodus of the Serbs, that issue and other issues and questions in the elaboration of your research, did you cooperate with anybody from Serbia except for the lady that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were in touch with various organisations based in Serbia, some of which I have -- for which I have a very high respect. There are in Serbia some very high-quality human rights organisations that worked in very difficult conditions. I can mention the humanitarian law centre, Fond Za Humanitarno Pravo, the Helsinki Committee, the Belgrade Circle and the Belgrade Centre for Human Rights, Lawyers Committee for Human Rights, among others. And we were -- we were cooperating with many of these organisations and individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that some of those individuals were also activists in the role of self-deprecation and self-accusation of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak to their personal psyches or the role they played in society other than that I considered many of them to be high-level professionals who worked at great risk to report objectively, something that was not easy to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that the Serbs, on the 24th of March, 1987, in Kosovo Polje demonstrated because they were maltreated by the Albanians. Is that correct? What kind of abuse and maltreatment was it, in fact?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you just repeat the question? I just didn't catch it precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the Serbs, in 1987 in Kosovo Polje, demonstrated because they were mistreated by the Albanians. What kind of mistreatment was this? You said you established that. What kind of mistreatment did you establish?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a degree of discrimination and maltreatment by the local authorities against Serbs. Primarily, this was what I would call a -- sort of ongoing harassment. But this was not a broad pattern of abuse. It was not an extreme abuse, in my opinion. The Serbian community in Kosovo, I think, felt itself very isolated. It was far from Belgrade, far from the heart of Serbia, the geographic centre of Serbia, and they were a minority within Kosovo. So this caused various pressures and was, in my opinion, the motivation for the demonstration to which you are referring.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right. Do you consider it to be logical that in Serbia Serbs should feel themselves to be a minority and should accept being mistreated in the kind of way that you have just explained them to have been mistreated? And let me add this: Do you consider that this was just some sort of -- what did you call them? Benign forms of mistreatment, I think you said. Harassment when they included rapes and killings and various other crimes of that nature. Yes or no. Arson as well.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will not belittle any violation of any sort. And the citizens of Yugoslavia had a right to be protected from these violations. The government should -- should pursue all measures to guarantee these protections, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where's the problem, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What problem?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem when the government undertakes measures to protect the citizens from terror, persecution, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why, then, is the government, for doing this as a legitimate act, accused of almost carrying out a crime? Not almost but accused of a crime.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, the problem is not that the government acted. Again, as I said yesterday, the problem is how the government acted. The government has the right to protect the rights of its citizens. Of course the government is obliged to do that. The government has a right to respond to an armed insurgency. But the government does not have a right to violate its own laws, to violate international norms when pursuing those actions, and that is our criticism of what happened in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you something, please, because you say that all of these are violations committed by the government. You are a New Yorker. How many killings and rapes, for example, are committed every day in New York?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't answer that. Yes. Now, Mr. Milosevic, the time is now coming to a close for your cross-examination. If you have another relevant question, you can most certainly ask it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have many more relevant questions, Mr. May, and I truly do not understand why you are restricting my time, even with regard to this witness, who is a live witness, not one of those famous "bis" witnesses. Why are you restricting my time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we are not going to argue about this now. Your time is restricted for reasons that you know, because the time in the case is limited, but more seriously, because of the amount of time that you spend on irrelevancies and arguing with witnesses and repetition, and we've just been having examples of it. Now, you can ask two more questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not that I've been arguing with the witness. I haven't noticed that. That must be your impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You wrote, on page 6, in paragraph 6, that the Assembly of Kosovo, on the 2nd of July, 1990, proclaimed Kosovo an independent constituent element of Yugoslavia. As a researcher, did you ever read the constitution of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the relevant sections that pertained to human rights protections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you've read it, on the basis of what can some kind of an assembly of Albanian separatists be given the status of the parliament of Kosovo, where not only Albanians live, but also Serbs, Roma, Gorani, and many other ethnic groups? Don't you know that this was an illegal enactment? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- the organisation Human Rights Watch never took a position claiming that it was legal or illegal. We stated it as a historical fact that this had taken place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this text that we've been quoting, you said that a message should be sent to dictators that their violence and lack of respect for human lives will not be tolerated, that they should not hope for that, because the international community will not allow this, only for the purposes of territorial integrity. Do you know that the question of territorial integrity of states is the governing principle of international law, respect for the territorial integrity of every country? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that territorial integrity is a crucial principle in international affairs, but our job as an organisation was to document and report on violations of the law, violations of domestic and international law, and in the case of Kosovo we argued that these violations were massive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm bringing that to a close. You have now had the hour you were entitled to. Do the amici have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Questioned by Mr. Wladimiroff:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, the Court has ruled on previous occasions that investigators are not allowed to testify about their assessment of events by passing to the Court their summaries or interpretations of what others have said or witnessed, so it seems to make sense to be very accurate on what you say what you witnessed and actually what is your assessment what others may have witnessed. In your evidence, you say repeatedly "our conclusion," "we found" or "we did not find," "we believe," "we reported," we this, we that. So what I'm going to do is ask you a few questions about the exhibits that have been tendered. Let's start with Exhibit 145, that is, the book "Under Orders." You have not written all parts of that book, have you?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court which chapters are written by you?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The book was primarily written by myself and Benjamin Ward, another researcher. Would you like to know chapter by chapter?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. Only those written by you.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: By me. I wrote the executive summary, the background, Forces of the Conflict, parts of the overview, I believe about half of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you specify?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which parts? Yes. I wrote the part on the killings, death toll, targeted killings, arbitrary arrests, contamination of water wells, and land mines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And please, do go on with the other chapters.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote the chapter on Djakovica, on Istok, on Orahovac, Pec, the Prizren-Djakovica road, Suva Reka, Vucitrn, the statistical chapter, and some parts of the abuses after June 12th, but that was mostly done by Mr. Ward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And work of the War Crimes Tribunal, and the legal standards I did, in cooperation with our legal office at Human Rights Watch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, looking at those paragraphs you wrote yourself, were these writings the results of what you witnessed by your own fact-finding or were you summarising, editing, evaluating the work of others?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which sections are you referring to? Because there are some differences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you told the Court which chapters have been written by you.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm asking you now which parts of these chapters you wrote were written on the basis of what you witnessed, or were these chapters written on the basis of what other people witnessed and you summarised their reports, evaluated their reports, or edited their reports, and you passed the information, through your book, to the Court?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a combination. Whenever possible, we visited the violation --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, please do not say "we." I'm asking you questions.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Me. Sorry. Yes. I visited a number of the crime scenes, such as Cuska village, Velika Krusa village, Bela Crkva. Otherwise, the findings are based on our interviews.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "our interviews"?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. By my interviews. The sections that I wrote were based primarily on the interviews that I conducted. However, there were some -- a few sections -- for example, I recall the village Belanica, or Gornja Studime, that were researched by other individuals, and I collected their notes and wrote the section in consultation with them. There are two or three villages like that. Otherwise, I did the research myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's elaborate that for a moment. When you write about the work that has been done by others, do you summarise what they have? Do you interview these people? Do you evaluate their reports? How does the process work?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The process works like this: We are in touch during the research and discussing the preliminary findings and the approach to the work, but most of the communication is afterwards. All of the interviews are typed up and reviewed carefully by myself and then written up, in consultation with the researcher who did them. This was the case -- I believe it was in the three villages that I mentioned: Belanica, Gornja Studime, and Trnje also. Those were three cases that were researched by someone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "writing up," does that mean you summarise what you have read or you evaluate what you have read or you interpreted what you have read?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that I wrote up their findings. That's the best way I know how to express it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Meaning you adopt their conclusions?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We stated the findings that they had obtained through interviews in the field. "They." It's one person I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's go through the exhibits, then, and start with 188, which is your report on Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: May the witness be given that exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, while that's being located and handed to the witness, it may just be worth observing with the premise that Mr. Wladimiroff is advancing, the premise that investigators are not allowed to testify about their assessment of events, it's possibly to overstate findings of the Court so far, which has been to the effect that investigators of the OTP are not allowed to summarise materials of others, because of course the Court has expressly allowed for both this document and also other documents from the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 40 of that exhibit, you will find the acknowledgment.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking that you took a part in this report by doing fact-finding missions yourself, and you also took a part in this report by writing and editing the findings of others?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report is based on a three-week mission I conducted in Kosovo, travelling around through the various villages of the province, and the findings are based on that research. I would have to look through the report to be precise on answering your question, but I can state unequivocally that secondary sources, reports from other organisations, I believe -- you know, these reports were perhaps cited, but the crux of our findings was the research that we did ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "we," you mean --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Me. Excuse me. Me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Let's go to Exhibit 190. There you will find the acknowledgment on page 29. Again, the same question: What was your participation in this report: fact-finding, writing about the work of others, or a mixture?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report was based on research that I conducted over a two-week period in Serbia, to interview the -- essentially, the victims and the witnesses of police abuse after the election of 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to Exhibit 191. There the acknowledgment you can find on page -- where was it again? Perhaps you could help us. Well, actually --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The very beginning, yes. I've got it in front of me. Written by you, but was it also based on what you witnessed?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report is -- primarily is based on my research in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by "your research," you mean you've spoken to the people yourself, you've been there on the spot, or is it you summarise or pass through what others actually have done on the ground?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily this was based on our research in the field, but as I said, there are cases when we cited the work of others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you say "our" and "we" --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm used to institutional affiliation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, yes, is based on my research. But as I said, we do occasionally cite the work of others. When we do cite the work of others, we are explicit in that. We give the reference, we provide the source.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you say "sources of others," do you mean people not working within Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. For example, another organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My questions are related more specifically to reports or findings or what was witnessed by those who work within Human Rights Watch and whose report you have seen. Have you seen all the events or have you relied on what has been seen by others working within Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The findings that we present as our own are based on our research in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you do you mean by "our"?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Based on my research in the field, or the research of my colleagues, but ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, could you clarify the additional research which is mentioned on the same page and done by Mr. Bouckaert and some other people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In this report there is research conducted by colleagues. Peter Bouckaert is a researcher who worked on specifically the Gornje Obrinje and Golubovac case, which are included in the appendix, yes, the appendix of this report. Would you like me to explain the other individuals, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're colleagues of Human Rights Watch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to Exhibit 198, please. That's the other booklet. Again, I'll ask you to look at the page dealing with acknowledgement, which is almost the same place as in the previous book. Here it says that on three field missions. These were done by you, conducted by you. What about the other admissions or were there no other missions that are reported in this report? And may I draw your attention to the Racak report.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report on Gornje Obrinje and Golubovac is based on three missions, was three missions conducted by myself and Mr. Bouckaert, but you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Excuse me. There's a problem with the transcript. I don't know if the Chamber is suffering the same problem, and I don't know if it's going to come back, so I just thought I'd mention it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we have any assistance on that? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This book is based on the three field missions. But you are correct; the appendix, which includes the report on Racak, was based on a fourth mission, so the acknowledgments are slightly inaccurate in that regard. That mission to Racak was conducted in the end of January 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you investigate Racak yourself?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you been in Racak?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on, then, to Exhibit 200. Would you please explain to the Court whether this is written on the basis of your own experience, what you witnessed, or is this a report written on the basis of what others did, not you?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report was researched by another person who was working for Human Rights Watch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. 201. That's the report about "Abuses Against Serbs and Roma in the New Kosovo." I may draw your attention to page 18. Were you involved in this report?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the part you took in this report?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report was primarily researched and written by Benjamin Ward, a researcher at Human Rights Watch. I contributed to the research. Particularly I recall conducting research among the Roma population. And I also assisted in the writing essentially as an editor for the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. 202, please, which is the report on "Kosovo: Rape as a Weapon of 'Ethnic Cleansing.'" And here may I draw your attention to page 38. The acknowledgement indicates that you edited this report. Question: What was your part in writing or researching the report?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the primary research was conducted by Martina Vandenberg with assistance from Joanne Mariner. My role was as a -- let's say advisory partner. Mrs. Vandenberg came to Kosovo in August 1999 when I was also there conducting research, and we spent a considerable amount of time together discussing this report, strategising on ways to conduct the research. And I also assisted her in some of the research. I recall that I did an interview with a doctor in Djakovica, for example. But the interviews with women were obviously conducted by Ms. Vandenberg herself and Ms. Mariner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed then to Exhibit 204, which is the report on "Detentions and Abuse in Kosovo." The same question: What was your part in this report?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the sole researcher and writer of this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. We move on to 206 -- excuse me, 205, which is the yellow booklet. Page IX. What was your part in this book?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do we have the same?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We do have the same.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Roman IX?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, Roman IX. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not working at Human Rights Watch during this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you very much. Finally, Exhibit 206, "Civilian Deaths in the NATO Air Campaign." There I draw your attention to page 79 -- 78, that is. Could you tell the Court what your part in this report was.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh. I conducted the research related to Kosovo of the 90 incidents of NATO bombings that caused civilian casualties. Approximately one-third of those incidents were in Kosovo itself. I did some of the research. For example, Dubrava Prison or on the road outside Djakovica, I did the research for that. Mr. Arkin and Mr. Ivanisevic did the research that was in -- outside of Kosovo, in other parts of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, two questions: There were two sets of letters tendered by the Prosecution. One is Exhibit 189. Just very quickly I'll show them to you. These were letters that you drafted yourself and were sent by yourself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The other set was Exhibit 192. Were these letters drafted by you and sent by you?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But signed by someone else.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were signed by my director, but I drafted them and sent them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also checked on these letters, whether there was any response or not?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I ask. You have been very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Probably about five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It would be more convenient, if we can, to finish. Re-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, the other researchers you've been dealing with in answer to questions from Mr. Wladimiroff, are they likely to be available and contactable should he want to make contact with them?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You'll help with that, will you, so he can track them down, if necessary, in case the suggestion is that any of them become witnesses?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I can do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to your reports, various reports, some of them -- we can see many of them were prepared and sent to various addresses well before there was any question of bombing of Serbia or Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In respect of that period of time when these earlier reports were being published and sent to different people, was there any suggestion of explicable bias levied against Human Rights Watch by the accused or any of the organs of government with which he was associated?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any direct accusations levelled at us directly from the government. Certainly there were responses in the press questioning our objectivity from commentators and other individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so that we can have the flavour, what sort of allegations of bias were levied against Human Rights Watch, and how, if at all, did Human Rights Watch respond to those allegations whatever they may have been?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's interesting that in the Balkans we've been accused of being anti-Macedonian, anti-Albanian, anti-Serbian, anti-Croatian, and in this case, we were accused of being anti-Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any reason given for it? I mean any explicable reason suggested by the accused that you were hand in glove with NATO now, I think, but all that could have been a possibility. Any other explicable reason given or was it just an allegation of bias?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume that it stemmed from a displeasure with our findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, so far as George Tintor is concerned, the author of the document, we've done our research while the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. cross-examination has been going on because the witness was unable to help us with anything about him. He, I think, checks -- he checks out to a website called antiwar.com and regularly writes letters to newspapers on the Serbian cause.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's been suggested that Human Rights Watch is supported only by the rich. Do you have support from people with less than $5.000 to give?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do students support you? Do young people support you?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Five thousand dollars is the amount above which donations are reported in the annual report. But of course many contributions below that amount also arrive. I can recall even envelopes with pocket change coming into the office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Under Orders." You've been asked about the amount that you wrote and the amount written by others in some detail. Where there were interviews of other researchers, did you review that material yourself?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in-depth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the stage of preparing for publication of the book, did you review the chapters prepared by your colleague? Did he review the chapters prepared by you?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to contribute by way of suggesting corrections where things were, in your judgement, in need of correction or reconsideration?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was very much a collaborative project.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You tell us that Human Rights Watch was aware of discrimination against Serbs in the 1980s. Can you help us with whether that's published -- whether that's covered in any of your reports or was that really too early to be touched on in any of the reports that you've drawn to our attention?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That period is covered in the background sections of some reports. Most concretely in the "Under Orders" report. It's in the chapter on background.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One matter of detail that you may be able to help us with: We've heard evidence -- I don't know if you can help us one way or the other about it. We've heard evidence of a time when Kosovo Albanians were losing their government jobs or their jobs in the banking sector and matters of that sort, to be replaced by incoming Serbs. Have you any knowledge of that? Have you dealt with that in any of your reports?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My work personally deals with that issue tangentially. The only report was the 1996 report where I talk about discrimination. We document discrimination in education and employment. But prior to me, I believe this report "Open Wounds" is the most exhaustive documentation of the period you are -- you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exhibit 205. And does that cover, do you recall, this process whereby Serbs were incoming and taking advantage of dismissed Albanians' jobs? And if you don't remember, just say so and we'll check it out.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It documents the discrimination in various sectors of the society.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What matter of detail, please. Can you take Exhibit 198, which is the -- that coloured one. At page 76. As you explained to the Chamber, the accused's quotation was from the press release from the 29th of January of 1999 in relation to the events in Racak, and the accused took you to a passage which was the second paragraph, where the press release referred to indiscriminate attacking of civilians, torturing of detainees, and summary executions, and you were asked how that was supportable. Would you please now take Exhibit 200, which is the short report prepared by a colleague and to which you did not contribute. I mention this simply because, in this Chamber, we're not in a position to explore all events in Racak, having to focus on a limited number because of the scale of the incident. If we -- if you have this report of your colleague, we can see on page 2, at the foot of the page, your colleague sets out on the basis of live interviews or interviews with survivors that she had conducted, and she sets out the number of interviews, at the foot of the page Torture, and she goes on there to say what happened in the yard of Sadik Osmani. That goes over on the top of the next page where she sets out in detail, and I'll allow the Chamber perhaps to read it for themselves, if they have it, to save time. She sets out an account of what happened to boys in the yard. And then in the third paragraph, people were searched for weapons, boys were taken out, and the way they were dealt with and so on. So was there material contained in this report to justify the allegations of torture and all the other allegations contained in the press release?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report is based on one week's research in and around Racak by Human Rights Watch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was with surviving witnesses, and it was, as it were, close to the events at the time?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. A matter of geography next which we can deal with in the same exhibit, because the Judges expressed an interest in the geography of Drenica specifically. If we look at the front of the document, there's a map which shows the location of Gornje Obrinje, Golubovac, and Plocica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not a page number. It's immediately after the index. So sorry. The map looks like that. The Chamber will find these places marked in our exhibit, the road atlas, as it were, at page 6. And it's in this square here, the bottom left-hand square of the right-hand page, and you can see the three places, Plocica, Golubovac, and Gornje Obrinje just in the square above. So that's where they're located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only description in your work that I've been able to find of Drenica can be found in Exhibit 191 at page 18. It's a short quotation where you describe or the authors describe Drenica as a hilly region in Central Kosovo. Are you able to assist the Chamber at all with the borders of the area known as Drenica or is it as general as that?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drenica is a region, not a municipality. So I'm not -- I'm not aware of the precise borders. But generally speaking, Drenica stretches from Kormnjan [phoen] near Glogovac - approximately I'm speaking - north to Srbica, and it's bordered on the east by the Cicavica Mountains, stretching west probably 30 or 40 kilometres in the direction of Pec.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I think I noticed Drenica on page 156 in "Under Orders."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Previously left in my room today, but I'll get the Court's copy. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It comprises -- Drenica stretches between the two municipalities of Srbica and Glogovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry not to have pointed that out to you earlier. I think I have two more questions, one relating again to Exhibit 198 about which you were questioned extensively by the accused. At the time of the publication of this report in February, had the bombing started or not?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the bombing had not started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The whole book was prepared and published before the bombing that it said it supported had even started.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were criticised yesterday, I think, for your failure to produce photographs of damage done by KLA and NATO. You said such photographs existed and had been considered by you. Do you want to tell us either, (a), in which report we should look to find them, or do you have a raw supply that you'll provide if they're relevant and if the Chamber wants to see them?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In brief, the photographs of KLA violations are included in "Under Orders," in the chapter "Abuses After June 12th." I believe there are also -- I can give page references if --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just in general, so we know --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK CRONIG ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In addition, there are photographs of KLA abuses on page 50 in the background chapter. There are two photographs in there. And regarding NATO, the -- the report on Civilian Deaths in the NATO Campaign has a series of photographs, more than a dozen, I believe, of damage caused by NATO bombs. And some of these -- those photographs are reproduced in "Under Orders."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Mr. May, I have an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are free to go. Yes, quickly, what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I have objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, quickly, what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Very quickly. [Interpretation] You did not allow me to get to my objections, having objected and questioned to all these exhibits which are mere publications and all -- and as I do, I challenge all these photographs. They cannot be exhibits of any kind. They have no probative value, nothing to authenticate them, nothing to prove who these people were, nothing to show whether they are even citizens of Yugoslavia, who these Albanians are, who the dead bodies were, who killed them. And the witness was not in Orahovac when the fighting went on, nor was he in Prekaze on the 5th of March, 1998, nor was he in Racak on the 15th of January, 1999, nor was he in Likosane and Cirez in the days in which he is talking about, nor was he in Suva Reka, Gornje Obrinje when what happened there took place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm going to stop you. We have admitted -- we have admitted his report. We have admitted his photographs. He has identified the places where he says they were taken. We have admitted them. Now, what weight we place upon them will be a matter for us. Now, we're going to adjourn. Mr. Abrahams, as I say, thank you very much for coming. You are free to go. There is one additional matter - apologies to the interpreters for keeping them - and that is that tomorrow and Wednesday, we will sit at 9.30. We have the court for the afternoon, and we will go until just after 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I will make adjustments to the witness list accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I should have said tomorrow and Thursday. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we return to K12, a few necessary administrative matters. First of all, Mr. Walker of OSCE has been contacted, and I'm expecting to speak to him later this morning and hopeful that we can call him next week. In order to call him next week, we would need leave in respect of late service of the B/C/S version of his second statement. The second statement has been served on the accused the second we got it, I think, in English, but, as the Chamber knows, there's a considerable backlog of translation. Nothing much we can do about that. And he hasn't yet had the B/C/S version. I would ask that we have leave to timetable Mr. Walker for next week, notwithstanding that.
