We will do -- if so, we will do whatever we can to prioritise or add priority to the translation of his statement, but it seems to us that the Chamber would probably be assisted by having as much of the Racak evidence at a similar time rather than divided by a long tract of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is the translation available yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not yet. We don't yet know when it's going to be available. We've been simultaneously, I think, pressing that and trying to make contact with Mr. Walker. Ms. Graham is about to give me a note. The accused had it in English on the 26th of March. It should already have come back. So presumably it's only a few days away in translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, perhaps you could deal with that at least by the weekend so that he has a chance to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. Yes. We're expecting perhaps to get the ambassador, if he's available, to travel on the Sunday. Thank you for that. The second point, for information of the accused: We have finally received, through the authorities, Marinkovic's report on Racak. It's in Serbian and, indeed, I think, in Cyrillic. That's being translated and of course will be made available as soon as it can be. I dare say the accused already has access to it himself from other sources. I mention it at this stage, though, for this reason: There's a videotape that is part of the judge's report. It covers various things, including some footage of General Drewienkiewicz, who we've seen, and footage of the arms allegedly found in the course of the inquiry. I may wish to put this video to a witness I'm calling tomorrow, and I will attempt to provide a copy of the video to the accused and to the amici and to the Court today so that they have some advance chance of looking at it. There are some other outstanding matters that I realise are slipping in time. I don't need to deal with them in detail, simply to say that there were some outstanding newspapers, some outstanding unresolved exhibits, and one way or another, Ms. Graham and I and your staff will ensure that we aren't letting things slip too much so that we forget them. Can I turn to the three witnesses of whom you expressed some concerns yesterday? Mehmeti Agron was originally a 92 bis witness, and it was in those circumstances that the original order, January order, of the 11th of January, I think, which referred to witness statements of witnesses to be called in person to be disclosed, was not thought to apply to him or other witnesses of the same category. In the event, service of B/C/S versions of his ICTY statement and interview occurred after the trial commenced, but all disclosure was completed on the 25th of January. That's, in fact, before the trial commenced. It was actually before. So all service was completed on the 25th of January. Avdyli, the same situation applies, and he again was, from the beginning, a 92 bis witness. His statements in English were disclosed on the 25th of January, two of the three of them disclosed in B/C/S at that time, the third disclosed, when available, on the 3rd of May. And then there were additional non-ICTY statements which were disclosed on the 23rd of April. So we would respectfully submit that we are in compliance, so far as those witnesses are concerned, although Ms. Graham helpfully reminds me that for Mehmeti, it was only the English statements that were served in advance of the trial; the B/C/S came a little later. There's no prejudice to the accused. The third witness, Agim Jemini, is a witness who we've always intended to call live, and therefore we do need leave to do so. He's a witness who provides evidence of overheard radio communications from the loft in which he was hiding, and it seemed that that evidence would serve a particular purpose, not just crime base, but it had literally a higher significance because of what he was able to overhear. The decision made to call him was being made at the same time as decisions were being made to reduce, wherever possible, the witness list. His ICTY statements were first disclosed in English on the 1st of February, so that was before the trial started; the B/C/S versions on the 15th of March; and there was a second statement in English served on the 13th of February. But again, all a long time ago, and his name has been on the list, so notification of our intent to call him has always been provided, although we haven't formally applied for an amendment to the list. He's here. He's a witness who, in our respectful submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We shall allow him to be called.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you move from that, there's a Mr. Elshani. Are you proposing to call him? He's at the bottom of the list, described as "may not be called."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. Elshani we have cut from the list. Your Honour, as to 92 bis rulings, the Chamber has not yet ruled on either Mehmeti, the next witness, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have a distinct recollection that we have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case, it's our oversight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: On all those down certainly as far as Hendrie is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Well, then if it's permitted for them to be given by 92 bis, that's all I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- we need know. I'm grateful. There's K7 tomorrow, and I'm not sure what the view was on him. He may fall into a different category.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I don't think we have yet dealt with K7.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We are preparing for him fully today, he being in a different category, and we will, of course, simply abide the announcement of the decision. Your Honour, that brings me to one point. We recall Your Honour limiting the -- announcing a limitation to 45 minutes of cross-examination for the accused in respect of crime-base 92 bis witnesses, but it may be that the accused had yet to have an opportunity to address the Chamber on that point, and it may have been that was reserved for discussion. That apart, I come back to the witness who started off yesterday, K12, and would invite the Chamber to allow us to go into private session just for a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The reasons for private session were entirely limited and as I explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness, K12, you are now back here. You'll remember that you have taken a declaration to tell the truth, and counsel will ask you some questions. Examined by Mr. Nice: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: K12, I asked you yesterday about whether you had done national service. Do you remember answering that question? You said you had done.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K12
utterances.text: Is he asking me something? Is he asking me to confirm something? What is this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do national service in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K12
utterances.text: I did do my military service, and I think I said that yesterday. Please tell him, tell the Judge that I have had enough of this psychological processing for two days now, and I've been confused even more and more. I cannot testify on anyone's behalf today, and leave me alone. I'll go crazy this way. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness -- Witness K12. You must understand your position. You are in front of a court of law which has summoned you to give evidence. You have declined to do so. We have considered our powers in relation to this, and they are these: that we may, in the exercise of our powers, hold in contempt those who knowingly and wilfully interfere with the administration of justice, and that includes any person who, being a witness before a Chamber, perversely refuses or fails to answer a question. Now, you should understand that we have a power to hold you in contempt for refusing to answer the questions which have been properly asked by the Prosecutor. Now, are you going to answer the questions or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If they think I'm guilty of something, then they can put me into prison. If they don't understand why I cannot testify, then I can't explain it any better than this. I've tried to explain this, but if I cannot, I cannot. And if they should think I should go to prison, I'll go to prison, and I'll sit there for as long as it takes. I have more problems now than if I were in prison. So just put me in prison, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. You are refusing to answer the questions of the Court. We make a finding that you are in contempt of this Tribunal as a result of your refusal to answer questions. We direct the Prosecutor to initiate proceedings against you. We will order the Registrar, if you make an application, to provide counsel for you. You will return to this Tribunal to be dealt, when your explanation or explanations of counsel will be considered, and we will decide what is an appropriate punishment for this contempt. Meanwhile, you will remain on the list of witnesses as a witness who is listed to give evidence. Should you change your mind and decide to give evidence, you should notify the Prosecutor, and you will be called. Meanwhile, you'll be notified of a date for you to appear here again to be dealt with for your contempt. The Court will now rise for five minutes before continuing with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, might it be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Might it be prudent to identify a first return date for the witness and for those who have to know about his return to the court on the basis that if we cannot meet that first return date for any reason, we will adjourn it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. A month. Twenty-eight days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We will find the date and the calendar and agree with the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Twenty-eight days. The Court will adjourn for five minutes. --- Break taken at 11.39 a.m.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Mr. May, I have an objection before we start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to hear this particular -- does it relate to this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No. This has to do with what was going on a short while ago. I have a very serious objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll hear the witness. We'll hear any objection at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I know who the witness is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In a moment. Just read out the declaration, if you would. Somebody check the declaration is in the right language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you begin with your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Me? Examined by Ms. Romano:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Agron Mehmeti.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mehmeti, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: In the village of Recak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when were you born?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: 15th of July, 1976.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you a Kosovar Albanian?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Yes. I am an Albanian of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you work as a coordinator for the Mother Theresa Society?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: I have done. At the moment, I'm out of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mehmeti, you gave two statements for the Office of the Prosecutor. One on 12 December 1999, and the second one on 24th of August, 2001; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: The first is correct. Could you explain the second one again to me, if possible?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 24th of August, 2001.

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you attended a meeting on the 6th of February, 2002, where were present an office of this Tribunal -- a presiding officer for this Tribunal, and at that opportunity, the two statements were read out for you, and you were provided also with a copy in the Albanian language; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Yes. This was sometime at the beginning of February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had the opportunity to review the content of the two statements and ascertain that they were true and correct?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: They were accurate, and if -- I do have some slight explanations to make, if the Court will permit me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. We will do it in the proper manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The Prosecution would like to submit the two statements into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 207.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The summary of the witness statement is the following: The witness states that there were unprovoked attacks on the village of Racak by Serb forces in the latter part of 1998. During this time, there was shelling and there were several houses damaged or destroyed. On 14 June 1998, a Serb policeman was killed in Caraleva, which led to a crackdown on the Kosovo Albanian population who were no longer able to travel to Stimlje. On 25 July 1998, there was a Serb offensive on the village of Zborce, about six kilometres away. The village of Racak was then attacked. The witness evacuated his family to another village, during which they were shot at by Serb forces. On 23 August 1998, the Serb police and army started firing at the village of Racak. The villagers took refuge in Shukri Hajrizi's basement but were later removed by the police. The head of each household was taken away by the police and their houses were searched. Around 80 houses were set on fire. On 15 January 1999, the witness's uncle, Bajram, woke him as he had heard explosions in the village. The witness then heard gunfire. He went to take shelter in Idriz Hajrizi's house next door. There were other people seeking refuge there, some of whom decided to flee in the vehicles of Veshta. En route, they were fired on. The witness's cousin Elham was injured in the leg. Bajram was shot in the head, and Hanemshah were shot in the chest. Both Bajram and Hanemshah died. The survivors took refuge in a house until dark, when they went to retrieve the bodies of the deceased. The following day, the witness learned that there had been a massacre in the village. Can I have the witness shown the Racak binder, tab 7. There are a series of photos in this tab. I would like the witness to be shown -- it's in the middle of the tab. It's crime location 3, scene 7. The ERN number is K0214950. I will start with photo number 1. It's the following sheet. Mr. Usher, if you can put this photo on the ELMO for the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, very briefly, can you explain to the Court what is in the photo, what you can see.

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: The photograph is of the village of Recak, and this is the lower neighbourhood, round the village mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you show where you were or where happened -- where Bajram and Hanemshah died or where did you took -- did you take refuge?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: The houses where we took shelter are not visible on this photograph. I think I need another photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can we move to photograph number 6.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I have objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are these photographs which were taken by Kelly? Because I can see the crime scene denotes "Crime Scene 1" and "Crime Scene 2." Those are Kelly's photographs, are they? And I understood that the witness was rejected. So how can we be using his photographs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The photographs have been admitted. The binders have been admitted. The fact that it says "Crime Scene" on it is totally irrelevant. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. [Interpretation] This is in order. This photograph relates to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, Witness, before -- before we check -- we change already to photo 6. Can you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you explain to the Court what is in the photo 6, what is in this photo?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain, if the Court will allow me to make a short explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: This is -- this photograph was no doubt taken after the war, because I can see a change here. This pipe was not here, placed in the stream, was not there. It was put there in the year 2000 or 2001.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm sorry. What I want you to tell the Court is what is this location? What does this location refer to during 1999? The changes Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. are not relevant.

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Yes. Only the pipe wasn't here -- there at the time, that iron pipe for -- to carry water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tell us what happened in relation to that scene.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the place where my uncle Bajram was killed. He was -- and my uncle's daughter Hanemshah was also shot dead. And then Hani Mehmeti was also wounded. Makfire Hajrizi was also wounded. This stream, we all jumped into this stream with the exception of Bajram. Hanemshah was able to walk for about five or six metres, and -- and while jumping into the stream, this is where Makfire Hajrizi was wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And are the two persons that you mentioned, Hanemshah and Bajram, are the persons in photos 8 and 9?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: I don't see the photographs, but no doubt they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The usher will provide you.

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, this is Hanemshah, 22 years old, Bajram's daughter. And this is Bajram, 54 years old. If you wish, I can explain when these photographs were taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. That's not -- that's not necessary, Witness. I just would like you to go back.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: If the usher can put again photo number 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I just would like you, if you can, show to the Court in that big photo where it's located. Where did it happen? Can you see in this photo?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: It's not in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then photo number 2.

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Idriz Hajrizi's house over there?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: What I can see here are the houses of the mosque neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Witness, when you gave the second statement to the Court, you were -- investigator Kelly, Barney Kelly, provided you with several photos of unidentified bodies, and you identified one by one. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: All these massacred people from the village of Recak whom I identified, I'm able today to identify them again today, if the Court wishes, by their first and second names and their dates of birth. And I could say two or three sentences about each person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, Witness. It's not necessary. I just want you to confirm if the photos that I will show you right now are the photos that were shown to you and that's the ones you made the identification. And I --

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Those photos are not in the Racak binder, and I have copies here, but I will need the colour copy back again to produce more colour copies. These are the colour ones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor, if you allow me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No. If you will just allow me. I don't think we need to go through all this evidence. We have the binders.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I just said they're not in the binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. Well, very, very quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I will not go through the identification. The identification has already been made in the statement. I just want the witness to confirm that these are the photos that were shown to him at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Would you just look at the photographs for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This person I see here, RA170 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't need -- you have already done the identification. You just need to tell the Court if you have seen these photos before.

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Yes. Can I go through them?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. You have already. Thank you. You've done this. It's not necessary. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Prosecutor, if -- it's not clear to me when we saw the photographs of where we set off on the 15th January and when we left the Hajrizi house. May I see them now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the Prosecutor decide what is relevant. We are having to adopt here, because of the shortage of time, rather abbreviated procedures. We're grateful to you for coming to give evidence, but I'm afraid we can't hear every detail. Ms. Romano, is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No. I just think that he was confused with the first map, with the first big photo, because previously, in proofing, he identified that map as the house, so I think he was a little bit confused. But that's not a big issue. I think we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've heard us say that we intend, for witnesses who deal with the various crimes under Rule 92 bis, their statements having been admitted, that we are intending to restrict your cross-examination to three quarters of an hour. The reason is that we've had experience of your cross-examination now over the last few weeks. A great deal of time is taken up with repetition and argument and sometimes irrelevancies. Now, do you want to say something about that, as to why we shouldn't restrict you in that way?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, I do. Because you're referring to experience, experience from the previous cross-examination, then you could draw from that experience just one conclusion, and that is the following: that there was one hour of cross-examination which was, without a doubt, insufficient, because for all witnesses that I cross-examined, within a limited time of one hour, you interrupted me, leaving many questions not asked. And so now, instead of increasing my time for cross-examination, based on what you have learnt from that experience, you are shortening the period at the request of the opposite side, that has trouble with time and sticking to timetables, so that the problems of the opposite side you are solving by restricting my cross-examination and limiting my time. So I continue to object to my time being curtailed and I continue to demand that it be -- that I be given at least one hour, which even that I consider to be insufficient. And you were able to see yourself that when I did not have many questions to ask witnesses, I would cross-examine them for quite a lot less than one hour, so I did not avail myself of that one hour you accorded me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I will deal with this matter and those issues which you raise. First of all, there is no truth in your suggestion that this rule was made at the application of the Prosecution. It was not. It was purely based on the time which you've wasted in your cross-examination. And the reason that you are interrupted, and will be if you continue, is because you ask either lengthy, repetitious, or argumentative or irrelevant questions. If you do that, you will be interrupted; if you don't, you won't be. Having had the experience of the last few weeks, when, I think out of the 67 witnesses, 66 that we've heard, I doubt if there are more than two or three that you haven't taken up any moment or any time that you are allowed, but two or three, if that, have gone short. So for those reasons, we shall restrict you to three quarters of an hour from now on for these witnesses. Yes. Well, it may be convenient now, in fact, to take the break before we begin the cross-examination. We'll break now for a quarter of an hour. Mr. Mehmeti, you are giving evidence. Don't speak to anybody during the break, please, about it until it's over. We'll be back at half past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First let's begin with the questions that were linked to the oral --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't need the binder any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said a moment ago the unjustified attacks on Racak in 1998. Is it true that nobody got killed in those attacks?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: In 1998, nobody was killed in Recak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that the police went searching for weapons during what those -- as you call them, unjustified attacks?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: I don't know whether the police were looking for weapons. They came on the 23rd of August, 1998, and burned 80 houses in our village and took two people with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with respect to what you said, that on the 14th of June, 1998, a policeman was killed, do you consider that it was unjustified for the police to come searching for weapons and to seek out the killer of the policeman?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: The policeman was not killed in Recak, and I don't know what kind of a question this is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, a moment ago, you yourself said that on the 14th of June, 1998, a policeman was killed.

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: I said that it was suspected that he was killed, but he wasn't killed in Recak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he was killed somewhere round Racak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: It is suspected that he was killed in Caraleva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the consequence of this was that the police was present and that you couldn't travel to Stimlje. Why weren't you able to travel to Stimlje?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: No. No. The police were there before, but there was a policeman killed, if indeed he was killed. There was a post block at -- there was a checkpoint and there was the army that was sited at the Pishat of Shtime, and there was no way we could get to Shtime. I don't see any point in going through these.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you could pass through the checkpoint. Were you able to pass through the checkpoint or not?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: No. To go to Shtime, no. There was a checkpoint at the crossroads, but I didn't have any reason to put myself in any danger. They -- there was no reason why I should put myself at risk in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you described the 15th of January by saying the following, and I want to ask you whether this is correct: You said that your uncle heard some firing, some shots, and that he fled to Hajrizi's house, and that some citizens were running, that one person was wounded in the leg, another in the head, and a third in the chest. That's how you described this whole event. And then you said that you heard later that there had been a massacre in the village. Now, is that what you said or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I could ask you to ask for the accused not to put such long questions, because I must give detailed explanations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is it that you don't understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, but if I have to answer such very long questions, it will take me a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just answer as best you can. We will get on more quickly if you'll just answer and don't get into arguments.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, but I don't know how to answer in brief to such long questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ask the witness another question, please, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in your first statement that your profession at the time when you made the statement was a coordinator for the Mother Theresa Society, and a moment ago, in response to a question asked by Ms. Romano, you said that you no longer worked for Mother Theresa. When did you cease working for her?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: I still have the badge of the Mother Theresa association here, if the Court needs to see it. I used to be a worker for the association, but at the moment, their association is not working because the emergency in our village has now passed and there is no aid -- no need for aid of this kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in addition to that, you said that you replaced the priest. Are you still his replacement?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: No. No, no, no. We Muslims don't have priests. We have an imam called a hoxhe, and I take his place at some times when he's not there. And I must -- and I must say here that I wish to see the transcript in Albanian. I've got it here in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what you're doing now too?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The transcript is only in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your statement, on page 1, in your first statement, you said the problem of Albanians in Kosovo became worse with the killing in the village of Prekaze, and they forced the Albanians to take on a peaceful action. Now, are you aware -- do you know that in 1998, a great wave of terrorism started? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: I don't understand this phrase "wave of terrorism," unless you're talking about your own police and army that committed acts of terrorism against the Albanian population. I can see no other meaning for this phrase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the terrorist operations of the KLA, which were numerous in 1998 and in which many people were killed, both Serbs and Albanians and other ethnic groups, soldiers and policemen. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: For me, the KLA is a liberation army, and I don't understand the phraseology you're using.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What the KLA did, is that what you refer to by saying that it was a peaceful action?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm talking about the civilian population which went in for peaceful demonstrations in the town of Shtime for 54 days on end. This is not an act of terrorism. We went out and protested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you about the KLA, and you said the Albanians were taking on peaceful actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're at cross-purposes. Just ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You link that up with the events in Prekaz. How far is your village of Racak from Prekaz?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: I can't say exactly in kilometres because Prekaz is in the north of Kosova and Recak is in the central southern portion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's about 70 kilometres. That's right, isn't it, if you go via Pristina and Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: No, no, no. I don't know exactly, but it's -- it's a long way and in an entirely different municipality. No doubt in Skenderaj municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the course of 1998 in the village of Racak and in the Stimlje municipality, were there any incidents, situations in which there were incidents of any kind?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: What I call incidents are the arrival of the Serbian police and army on 23rd of August when they burnt houses and expelled us from the places where we were. I don't know what else you could call an incident, burning people's houses merely because they're Albanians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, as a moment ago you questioned the killing of the policeman, you write in your first statement, on page 2, and I quote: "On the 14th of June, a Serb policeman was killed, and after that we were not able to go to Shtime." Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Not only that the Serbian police was killed. That's not the only reason. Even before it was suspected that the Serbian policeman was killed, the road was blocked and we were unable to go to Shtime for protests or even to buy our groceries, and this was what the police did. And if you're interested in evidence about whether the Serbian policeman was killed or not, I can provide some details and evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In the next paragraph, you say: "It seems that a policeman was killed in Crnoljevo." Are you describing the same killing when you say that? Do you have in mind the same killing, the same murder, or another killing?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: No. This is the claim, that there was a policeman killed there. On the basis of information that we had and heard on the television and were transmitted in Serbian, or it was sometimes translated into Albanian, it is thought that there was an incident at Caraleva where a Serbian policeman was killed, but I wasn't there in Caraleva, so I can't exactly tell you whether it happened or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that on the 25th of July, 1998 an attack was launched on the village of Zborce, my question to you is: Why were you in danger, when you say in your statement that that village is about six kilometres away from Racak?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: It's six kilometres from Recak. And from the Pishat of Shtime and Cesta and Podja e Geshtenjeve, they shelled the village of Zborc from these positions and also shelled Recak and other villages of Shtime municipality. We saw them shelling Zborc. We were not a thousand metres away from them. How should we not be afraid? Because in this kind of threat, we were unable to stay in the village. Think of the noise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say: "They shot at us from a hill. They did not hit us. But I do not think that they were intending to hit any one of us but rather to frighten the fleeing refugees." Do you still stand by what you said there?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Yes. This might be true. But just a moment, please. Please. Someone who is firing, this is an attempt at murder. I don't know how somebody can be -- with armoured vehicles. Is there anywhere in the world can it be allowed for this sort of thing to happen and people not be afraid?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the 2.300 inhabitants of Racak, how many of them were KLA?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Recak had 2.370 inhabitants. These were civilians. I don't know exactly how many were soldiers of the KLA, and I have no authority to speak on this. No doubt a witness will come who may be able to tell you properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But roughly speaking. Tell us roughly. Give us a rough estimate. You don't know exactly, but you have an idea, I assume, of how many, approximately.

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: I can't even really give you an idea, because I wasn't involved in the KLA and I didn't have lists, so I can't give you an exact figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you say in your first statement, on page 2, for the period Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. after the killing of the policeman on the 14th of June, and I'm quoting you: "The KLA was gradually coming into prominence and engaged the Serbs." So you do have an idea about this. Explain the meaning of that observation of yours, if you do not have an idea about it, as you now say.

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: The KLA, based on media reports of the time - that is what I relied on - it wasn't the liberation army of Recak or Shtime. It was called the Kosova Liberation Army, so it covered the whole territory of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you go on to say, after this, after saying the KLA was gradually coming into prominence, you go on to say that that is why the Serbs took energetic measures and carried out an aggression. Is that the point of your explanation, that the Serbs reacted to the activities of the KLA? Is that right or not? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: No, I can't have a yes or no answer to this, because I don't have a brief answer to give if the Serbian police and army took measures against the KLA, because -- and the orders came from yourself, from the accused to attack the village of Recak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said that because the KLA was gradually coming into prominence and engaged the Serbs, that that was why the Serbs took energetic measures and carried out an aggression. So what I'm asking you is: Is it true or not that the forces of the police reacted to the activities of the KLA? Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: I do not know. The KLA on a territory-wide Kosova. I do not mean the KLA in a village, in a neighbourhood, or something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that means your village too, and that's why I'm asking you: How many were there in your village?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: There were no soldiers of the Kosova Liberation Army in my village. As I said earlier, I can only reply here regarding civilians who I lived with in my village. If you've got any questions on those, I can provide an answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know how long the trenches are, the trenches that the members of the KLA had dug and used in the village of Zborce that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: No, I do not know. I haven't been there to see the trenches. But it's six kilometres away from Recak. I haven't been there to see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But a minute ago you said that you were watching the activities of the police from a distance of one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Pishat e Shtime is about a kilometre away, and as I put it earlier, it's fifty metres to a thousand metres away, north-west of Shtime, and from there, the village of Zborc was being shelled at. And I have -- I've seen the APCs, the Prikolica, and the Pragas shelling out. I've seen the shells coming out of there, but I haven't seen where they landed. It's quite a big difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that there were about three to four hundred people left in the village - I'm quoting you: "I had to keep the good name of my family, just like other men did at the time. They stayed behind in the village to protect their property." So 300, 400 men remained to protect their property. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: There were not only men who remained behind. There were also some other families who were not scared as much, and some stayed behind. In my statement, I said they stayed to look after their animals. And I cannot even understand this. It's absurd, as far as I'm concerned, to be evicted from my own property just because of ethnicity, because of being an Albanian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said yourself that you remained to tend to the cattle, the crops, that you were sending your family vegetables from the vegetable garden, et cetera. So what you say, is that proof of the fact that nobody impeded these everyday activities of yours and of the other men who had stayed behind in the village? Isn't that telling proof of this?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Unless were they not inhibited. I just cannot understand that. I did not say that. The threats were there, and it's only after the war that I have been able to come to terms with the whole wave of threats coming from the shells from your Serbian police and army. I mean, the threats, of course, were unable to prevent the growth of tomatoes and other groceries, other plants, because water comes of its own accord. All I had to do was take 15 minutes and go and tend to them. Maybe I'm wrong, but I don't think you can stop the growth of vegetables, because if you had that possibility, you would probably have taken it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that during that period, that is to say the summer of 1998, the police was shelling the hills although they did not enter the village. My question is the following: Why was the police shelling the hills?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: I think that you've got the wrong address. I think I should ask this question to you because you gave the orders, and you should know why the hills were coming under attack, and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there any KLA strongholds in these hills?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Which village do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to hills.

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: I do not understand which hills. Recak borders on Shtime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are your words. This is what you said. "The police were shelling the hills, although they did not enter the village."

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: No. They did not enter the village before 23rd of August, 1998. They were shelling over Recak and the houses in the neighbourhood. There were seven or eight cases, which have not been mentioned in that statement, of houses that came under attack by mortars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. After searching the houses, in this same period the policemen told you not to go into the woods, and they repeated the same thing to you before they left the village. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: What period of time are you referring to? What is the date? the month? the year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the period that you referred to in your statement. You said that when you wanted to leave the village to go into town - I'm quoting what you said - that you did not have to go anywhere because they would protect you. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Serbian police to protect us? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what you wrote in your statement. You said: "We didn't have to go anywhere because they would protect us." That's what they said to you. That is in your statement.

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where is this, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I haven't got the statement here with me, but it is certainly contained in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Page 4, last paragraph in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbs were willing ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you explain this, that, "the policemen called Bozha and Mira --" I'm quoting your words -- "were very well known and notorious in the town of Stimlje," when in your first statement, on page 3, you say: "One of the Roma wanted to attack us, but Mira said to him not to touch us, and that Mira stopped nudging us along with his rifle butt immediately." Isn't that right? That means that he protected you.

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: I think the names were confused. Mira, somebody else. Bozha, some -- another policeman. There are-- was another policeman. There were others. There was Sasa, Ceta. And I'm referring to the 23rd of August, 1998. They were wearing bandannas. He had the red armband. Mira had a red armband on his arm. And other policemen were just pushing us with the butts of their rifles, and Mira asked them not to do it. I think it was a game of theirs to play with us in a way that did not mean anything to me. They were all the same to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know Nazmi Luri or Olluri, an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Where is he from?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was killed by the KLA between the villages of Zborce and Balince at a place called Kodra Gorance. He was only three years older than you. He was born in 1973. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: No. No. Do not try and compare who is of the same age as I am. Bozha and Mira. You shouldn't try and compare your terrorists to myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just try and concentrate on the questions, if you would, Mr. Mehmeti. We'll get on more quickly. You were asked if you knew an Albanian who was killed. Do you know that man or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This person does not come from Recak. This name doesn't exist. I'm not aware of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Xheladin [as interpreted] Fehmi from Racak, born in 1954, who was abducted by the KLA on the 2th of December, 1998? An Albanian woman, Abazovi Fatime, born in 1958, reported the abduction to the MUP, to the police. This is a man from Racak. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One at a time, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you permit me on the first question, I can provide an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, did you know Xheladin [as interpreted] Fehmi from Racak?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... answer the question. Do you mean Fehmi Xheladini?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that he was abducted by the KLA on the 28th of December, 1998?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: No, he was not taken by anyone. I do not know where he was as a refugee at that time. After June the 12th, 1999, as everybody else from Recak, he came to seek humanitarian aid at my humanitarian society in Recak. In fact, today I don't know where he is, but I saw him a week ago at his own -- in his own house -- or, rather, outside his house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that his abduction was reported to the police, to the SUP, by Fatime Abazovi, an Albanian woman?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: There is no Fatime Abazovi in the village of Recak. This name does not exist. This information is wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that on the 10th of January, Svetislav Perzic, a policeman, was killed near Racak on the 10th of January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Did you say the 11th of January?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 10th of January.

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of any policeman having been killed. There was even -- no shooting at all during that period, because I think the alleged -- the accord with Holbrooke that you yourself signed was in force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. On the 11th of January -- well, this is what it says on page 5 of your statement. You said to your uncle -- you said to your uncle that your cousin Vehbi should be taken to Godance because "then it will be easier for us to run away if they attack us;" is that right? Did you already know about the police action then, and they had encircled the village in order to catch the killer of the policeman?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: I cannot understand why do -- you did not refer to January the 9th, not January the 11th, and I can't understand why you didn't read that. It was on that particular day that Serbian police came and stayed there, and that was the reason why I asked for Vhebi to leave the village, so that myself and my uncle could leave at very short notice in case anything happened like what happened on January the 15th by your own forces, at the hands of your own forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In the second statement, dated the 24th of August, on page 1 you explain that you took the investigator of The Hague Tribunal to show him, I quote what you said, that "the investigator should see the significant sites in Racak where people were killed on the 15th of January, 1999." My question is the following: Did you mark these sites without having seen any one of these killings personally? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: No. The sites -- I showed Barney Kelly the sites where me -- where I was present when my relatives were killed, where my uncle and her [sic] daughter. Whilst on other sites, what I showed Mr. Kelly was what had been told by other people, as was the case of Sahide Metushi, who was killed by your own police. And her body's -- her body disappeared and is still missing. The grave is still empty and the whole village of Recak is looking for that. And I have a question to you: If you know where that body is, can you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with that, I'm asking you -- it's precisely in connection with that that I'm asking you. I quote: "Shabani said to me that his mother had told him that she had seen the body lying there. Until the present day, the body hadn't been found." So you hadn't seen any of this. And Shabani told you that his mother had seen this; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I was about 200 metres away from the site of the killing. Now, I can call her missing. It is correct that that was related by Shabani's mother. To be more precise, the mother of Rame Shabani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that you showed the investigator the sites where Nazmi Nuha was allegedly killed? And this was on the basis of stories told by other villagers, but you hadn't seen it either?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: No. The alleged killing of Nazmi, I saw him elsewhere, not where he was killed. He was an elderly gentleman, unmarried, had no children. He was about 80 years of age. In my briefcase, I have got the exact date of birth, if the Court would need that. And he was massacred by the police. The police, the army, the paramilitaries; I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was related to the fact that you had not seen this yourself. You heard stories about it. This is based on the stories told by other villagers; right?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Yes. I have not witnessed this myself. I did not see the killing of Nazmi Nuha because I did not go alongside the policemen to see who they were killing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, but let us move on. And did you state the following in relation to Asllani, that the Serbs killed him on the 15th of January, but you do not know where, that somebody told you about this but you do not remember who it was that told you about it. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember who he was. I know he was killed. Mustafe Asllani, Mustafe Beqe Asllani, was killed. And he was a mentally retarded person. It's probably not in my statement. I did not say he was handicapped or mentally retarded. The word "mentally" is not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am just quoting your statement. And did you then describe the death of Halit Shaqiri [Realtime transcript read in error "Halil"] and Avdyl Demaj in your statement? And did you present to the investigator two versions of their killings and then you said, "I'm not sure which story is true"? Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I was not with Halit when he was killed. He was with his own uncle, Avdyl Demaj. They were killed in Shtime. I do not have the exact date, but I think it's 14th of April, 1999. I don't know what time this occurred. There were two versions given of this event. Whether it was the first or the second, I don't know. And that was all based on the information that I got from the family of Halit Shaqiri. I was more interested in obtaining information, given he came from Recak. I see a mistake here on the monitor. It's not "Halil," it's "Halit" with a "T".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From whom did you learn about both versions regardless of which one is correct and which one is incorrect or whether any one of them is correct? Who told you about these two versions?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: The family of Halit Shaqiri. The two versions are fairly similar. It's either the first or the second version that applies, and that shows that Serbian police killed these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, is it correct when you talk about the killing of Hasan Beqiri you actually talk about secondhand knowledge? It is something that you had not seen for yourself either. It's something that somebody told you about as well; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: The translation is not reaching my headset. I can't hear you. I can hear it now. I haven't seen Hasan Beqiri being killed on the site where he was. His body was brought to the village of Petrova, and I -- and I buried him with my own hands alongside some other inhabitants of Recak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And is it correct that this story about his death is something that you heard about from a young man? And in your second statement, you say, I quote: "But I don't know his name." You heard about this from someone whose name you do not know; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: I've now found out his name, after giving the statement to Barney. If required, I can give you the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But again, you heard about this from a person whose name you did not know then, but you hadn't seen this yourself either; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: I didn't see Hasan -- I didn't see a Serbian policeman killing Hasan. I saw him killing someone from the village of Dramjak. I took -- I saw Hasan from the village of Petrova and I buried him with my own hands, alongside some other inhabitants of Recak. Hasan -- the place where Hasan was killed is Caravik, near Petrova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he perhaps killed in the fighting between the KLA and the police? How do you know whose fire killed him, and how do you know anyway whose fire killed the persons that you are mentioning? How do you know about this when you hadn't seen any of it?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: I can refer you to Arben's information, and he told me that he heard the policemen talking in Serbian, and they both fired, and they struck Hasan in the stomach, while Arben managed to survive this murder. I buried Hasan in Petrova, and on the 30th of August, I exhumed him, and we buried him and two others in the cemetery of those who were massacred in Recak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it mean, "heard the Serb policeman"? What did he hear when he heard the Serb policeman?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Not the policeman, but the policemen. Arben heard them talking Serbian, and no doubt they were swearing, and they fired. And these people went to see the column of refugees to see where to send the paramilitaries and to see whether to send the refugees in the direction of Albania or to Macedonia. That's why they went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he heard them, but that had nothing to do with any kind of killing. He heard their conversation; right?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: I don't know whether you are trying not to understand me or not. These were young people. These were 15- or 16-year-old boys. I have the details here in my bag. And they wouldn't know Serbian very well, and I don't think that they went up to him to offer them sweeties. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, your time is now up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one more question to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, and this is on page 03045489: The house in which Avdyl was located was destroyed. You say the Serbs set fire to the house, and you say: "I did not see his body, but while I was carrying the box, I thought I was carrying an empty box." Is that what you say? Is that what you say in your statement?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Avdyl Sejdiu was an aged person, 99 years old, very, very worn out, and he didn't weigh any more than 40 kilogrammes. Yet your forces burned his house, with him inside it, in the village of Greme. And his family went and fetched the body, the skeleton, and when I lifted his coffin, it was like lifting an empty coffin, even though the bones were in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I take it you haven't got any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Just two matters, Your Honour. Re-examined by Ms. Romano:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in order to clarify the record, and it's also your statement, but can you mention the names of the persons you yourself saw being killed?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: I saw two people killed one metre from me. That's Bajram Mehmeti, 54 years old; and Hanemshah Mehmeti, 22 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen the bodies of the other people, the other people killed on 15 January, that day or the day after?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: The 42 civilians who were massacred on the 15th of January, between 7.00 in the morning and 5.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw their bodies?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Yes, the next day, apart from a few that evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you saw them where?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: What bodies are you asking about now? There were 24 massacred on the hill of Bebush.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you saw them in the hill?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Yes, on Saturday, when the distinguished Ambassador William Walker arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, but I will have to go back to the binder, just in order to -- in fairness to the witness, because the first photo that was shown to him was a wrong photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So I would ask the usher to show on tab 7 photo K0214951.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened and what is that location?

utterances.speaker: AGRON MEHMETI
utterances.text: Yes. This is Idriz Hajrizi's house here. That's my uncle's house, the house of Bajram Mehmeti. And here, in another yard, is my house. We were sheltered in Idriz Hajrizi's house, and at 10.25, Hasan Balalli came and said that the police and the army were entering the village. So we went out of this house and went along this road, this lane. And here Elhami was wounded. And my cousin Hanemshah shouted, shouted to my uncle, and said that Elhami was wounded. And my uncle arrived. And here the arrow shows where my uncle was hit by a bullet from Bebush hill. And he fell very near me and closed his eyes. And his daughter shouted again and said -- and the paramilitaries of the accused hit her in the chest. And then Arben, Arben Hajrizi, first jumped into this stream, and the others after him, and Makfire Hajrizi was wounded while jumping into the stream. Hanemshah, five or six meters, she was able to walk a short distance, and Ramiz Hajrizi helped her, and here she died and was left here until the evening, when the firing stopped. And we were sheltering here, in what you might call a larder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have read all this. Thank you, Mr. Mehmeti.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mehmeti, you just said that bullets were from Bebush hill. Was it right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. But they also came from the main road and from Cesta, from three directions. And on the basis of the wounds suffered by my uncle, you can tell that he was hit by a bullet that came from Bebush.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mehmeti. That concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I, for half a minute ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm afraid not. Our Rules don't permit statements from witnesses. We are much under pressure of time. But thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, in the name of the village of Recak and everybody there. May I now go and leave him here in the place where he deserves to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution next calls Xhemajl Beqiri.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, if - while we're waiting for this witness - if you would pass on the message as to Witness K7. I don't know if you're dealing with him or somebody else, but whoever. We've had a brief look at his statement, and he doesn't appear to be suitable for Rule 92 bis. But we'll hear evidence in due course about it or we'll consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. So in light of that ruling, the Prosecution will call him as a live witness, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, while we're waiting for the following witness to be brought in: In view of Your Honour's clarification that the documents that are in the exhibit binders have been admitted into evidence, I do not propose to take the next witness and take up further Court time with -- back to the Racak binders. I'm just going to have him -- I'm just going to read out a summary and have the attachments properly identified in the statements, available for the Court to look at at the Court's leisure, if that meets with your approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take the oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat, Mr. Beqiri. Examined by Mr. Ryneveld:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Beqiri, could you please tell the Court your full name.

utterances.speaker: XHEMAJL BEQIRI
utterances.text: Xhemajl Beqiri, from the village of Recak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do I understand, sir, that you've lived in Racak all of your life?

utterances.speaker: XHEMAJL BEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're 48 years old and you are of Kosovo Albanian ethnicity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: XHEMAJL BEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: XHEMAJL BEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many children do you have?

utterances.speaker: XHEMAJL BEQIRI
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I understand, sir, that you have formerly been a farmer, but in the last few years your occupation has been a taxi driver?

utterances.speaker: XHEMAJL BEQIRI
utterances.text: I used to be a taxi driver, yes. Now I'm a farmer again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I propose to read in a very brief summary, if I may. Your Honour, according -- well, actually, I should ask a couple of other questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, on the 7th of December, 1999, did you give a statement to investigators of the ICTY in regard to the incidents that occurred in Racak?

utterances.speaker: XHEMAJL BEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then in February of this year, on the 6th of February, did you appear before a presiding officer of this Tribunal and confirm, in a solemn declaration, that the statement you gave was true to the best of your knowledge, information, and belief?

utterances.speaker: XHEMAJL BEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might that statement at this time be marked as an exhibit in these proceedings, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And if Madam Clerk wants to give it an exhibit number, then I propose to read while that's happening.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 208.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, according to the statement which is just being distributed, prior to the January 15th, 1999 attack on the village of Racak, Racak had previously been the subject of various attacks by Serb forces. Now, on the 15th of January, the witness describes in a statement that at about 6.45 a.m., he woke to the sound of a blast in the village. He says he realised that the Serbs were attacking, and he and his family them climbed a hill to escape. There were refugees from Blinc in Racak, because their houses had already been burned the month previously. He describes in his statement Serb police coming in APCs and Pragas. He then identifies, via photographs which are marked as attachments to his statement, the type of artillery that the Serbs used on that day, and those again are available to Your Honours. Now, while apparently watching this artillery by the use of binoculars, watching the artillery coming towards the village, he noted that he got a bullet through his cap that he was wearing at the time. During the course of this attack, his relatives - Rame, Zenel, and Riza Beqiri - shot and killed, and Zyher and Fetije Beqiri, his mother and daughter, were shot and injured. He took refuge in Hysni Emini's house, where other villagers were also present. He describes in his statement that Esmet Emini came into the house with a gunshot wound to his hand and stated that the Serbs had killed Esmet's brother Ajet in front of his house. This witness could hear the sound of gunfire and people screaming outside. He describes that Serb police arrived and ordered them out into the street, whereupon he saw the bodies of his 54-year-old cousin Bajram Mehmeti and his 20-some-odd-year-old daughter Hanemshah lying on the road. Two of the witness's nephews, Beqe and Mehrem, were apparently in the KLA. Mehrem did not join the KLA until after the 15th of January incident, when his father Riza and brother Halim had been killed. He notes that there were regular police officers there that he recognised, but he was not able to name them by name, other than two. One was Bozo and one was Cvetko, last name unknown, who ordered them to line up in the street and insulted them. The men were then separated from the women. The Serb police accused the men of being KLA soldiers who had been shooting at them and threatened that they would be shot, and then they shot at one of the villagers, narrowly missing him. The men were ordered to go up a hill, but instead they walked towards the Berisha stream, but Serb police came from another direction and fired on them. They ran for cover and, fortunately, escaped injury. In an attachment to his statement, he identifies various shoulder patches that were worn by the police that he saw. He and his cousin brought the bodies of Riza, Zenel, and Halim back to the house of Shefqet and later moved them to the mosque, where about 40 other bodies had been collected. He later learned about 24 bodies having been located in the ravine on the day that William Walker from the OSCE arrived. He claims that there were a total of about 40 victims. Then he describes for you that on the 17th of January, two days after the assault, he and his family left the village for Luzha, which is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. two to three kilometres from Racak, and then describes how in the ensuing weeks they travelled to other villages, along with the other refugees. He states in his statement that there was no KLA presence in Racak on the day of the massacre. He explained in proofing that there was no KLA in his neighbourhood of Racak. Your Honours should know that Racak consists of various neighbourhoods. I think they are referred to as mahallas. He believes that the KLA came to Racak after the attack. He also heard that the Serbian investigating judge was permitted to visit Racak by the KLA, provided she was not accompanied by the Serbian police. He indicates that he was told that Serb police came to the village on the 18th of the 1st of 1999 and forcibly took the bodies to the Pristina morgue. He was told that most of the bodies were given back to the villagers about a month later, and he returned to Racak to participate in the funeral. He indicated that he remained in Kosovo throughout the conflict. That is a brief summary of the statement that Your Honours have been provided with, and he's now available for cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examination in the morning, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The objection that you said you would allow me to state regarding K12 at the end of today's day, what about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is not a matter for you. This was a procedure which the Court adopted. It had no bearing on any intervention on your part. What is it you want to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to take note of several facts. First, without a doubt, the witness K12 took the oath, the solemn declaration. Secondly, it is without doubt that he did start his testimony, because in the few minutes that he spoke, he answered several questions, and then that testimony of his was interrupted. According to your own Rules - and you draw everybody's attention to them - when a testimony starts and it is interrupted, the opposite side, or anybody else, cannot communicate with the witness, which in this case was not a provision that was respected, and I'd like to draw your attention to that and object to it. Secondly, he stated here, into the microphone, that for two days they processed him. Now, I should like to remind you that there is an international convention which guarantees that statements cannot be extorted from witnesses. And what he meant by "two days of processing," I consider it your business to ascertain. That's all that I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Prosecution are entitled, and the parties are entitled here, before a witness gives evidence, to speak to them and, if necessary, to take a further statement from them. So there was no irregularity there. Secondly, a party may, with the Court's leave, speak to a witness during the course of his evidence if it's necessary. In this case, the Prosecution were allowed to speak to the witness because he was refusing to give evidence. So there is nothing in your objection. No rules were breached. Now, we'll adjourn now. Mr. Beqiri, could you be back, please, at 9.00 tomorrow morning - I'm sorry, I'm reminded it is 9.30 tomorrow - to give your evidence. Thank you very much. And could you remember not to speak to anybody during the adjournment, and that does include members of the Prosecution team, and not to speak about your evidence until it's over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
